🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -0.57% (intraday, 7-year +8bp). At trading day 25 (last close) it was -0.57% against a five-campaign average of -1.46% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.63%. The 10-year is +10bp since the hike vs a +20bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 4 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 762bp against a five-year average of 413bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +71bp and BB +45bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.31 → 0.61 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is moving too (+11bp in a month).
  • Bank Earnings: 8 banks reported (COF, EWBC, HWC, NIC, BKU, NTRS, ONB, OZK); 3 red-flagged (HWC: NPLs +17% QoQ; BKU: NPLs +18% QoQ; NTRS: NCO ratio +11bp QoQ). Credit deteriorating at the margin; deposit costs flat. Watch: HWC, BKU, NTRS.
  • Stocks: US and European stocks rose; tech led and the Nasdaq gained about one percent.
  • FX: Currencies barely moved after the close; the dollar held flat and the yen stayed weak.
  • Technicals: Stocks sit just above their 50-day average trend line; oil and yields stay strongly up-trending, gold down.
  • Sectors: Tech led today, but energy and defensive sectors have led over the past month.
  • Credit/Spreads: Lowest-rated junk debt now pays its widest premium since April 2020; single-B and BB are following.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate; junk credit and the oil shock are the main pressure points.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is sticky near 3%, and energy keeps pushing prices up.
  • Tech Bubble: Stock prices aren't at 2000-style mania, but investors are as relaxed about risk as in 2000.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Alphabet is the biggest name reporting; Bloom Energy has the biggest expected price swing.
  • Iran: We found no news of the Iran war dated today; a ceasefire was reported earlier.
  • Warsh: Warsh won't say ahead of time what the Fed will do; we expect a hold next week.
  • Week Ahead: Next week brings the Fed's rate decision, third-quarter GDP, the PCE inflation report, and earnings from Microsoft and Alphabet.
  • Outlook: Short term neutral: stocks are firm, but stress in the riskiest debt could spread to stocks.
  • Trades: Own energy, move junk-bond holdings toward higher-rated issuers, avoid long-term bonds, and keep stock stops tight.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 3 buy, 23 hold long, 19 stay out
  • Regime Rules: S&P 500 risk-on; NDX risk-on, 7.0% above its sell trigger; trend intact; credit spreads widening
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.54 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 93th pctile, +18bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Stocks look fine, but the junk-bond market is flashing a warning worth respecting.

Wednesday's session was a tech-led bounce: the S&P 500 rose 0.5782768% to 7757.17, the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.052193% to 26702.86 and the Dow added 0.6861681% to 52856.09, while the Russell 2000 lagged at +0.274066%. Europe did better: the Euro Stoxx 50 jumped 1.402561% and the Nikkei rose 0.8518399%. Sentiment was calm. The VIX slipped 0.63 to 16.68, and Info Tech (+1.61% 1d) recovered after a weak month. The biggest story sits under the surface, in high-yield credit. The computed HY contagion panel (Bloomberg, as of 2026-10-20) has the Caa–B gap at 762bp, 100th percentile of its 5-year history against a 5-year average of 412.8bp, and the widest since 2020-04-23. Caa OAS is 1085bp (+167bp over 1m, +277bp over 3m). The stress is no longer confined to CCCs. Single-B widened +80bp over 1m to 323bp, BB widened +52bp to 201bp, and IG widened +11bp to 86bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes rose to 0.61 from 0.27 a month ago, still below its 0.70 5-year median. Read descriptively, that is the pattern of CCC stress spreading into single-B and BB. Single-B and BB levels are still only around the middle of their 5-year range (54.6 and 53.1 percentile), and IG is at the 37th percentile. So this is contagion in motion, not yet a broad repricing. It is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Headline HY OAS is only 3.32% (computed z-score -0.63, 24th percentile), which shows how concentrated the damage is. Rates were mixed: the 2Y rose about 3bp to 4.806% and the 10Y about 1bp to 5.119%, while the 30Y eased about 1bp to 5.4089%. Brent is at 110.07 and WTI at 97.15, keeping energy inflation in play ahead of next week's FOMC (Oct 27–28), Q3 GDP and PCE.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 476.33 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is at 476.33 cents/gal, a historic extreme: outright price sits at the 99.8th percentile and the crack spread is at a 5.53 z-score of 102.9086 $/bbl. Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

Widening velocity, not level. Near an all-time high a 63d widening past the trigger has historically raised P(SPX -10% within 3m) from ~8.6% to ~21.9% (Baa p=0.013, HY p=0.028, IG p=0.047, 1990-2026, corroborated on three independently-sourced series). The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. 💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.54 vol points (12th percentile of the 48 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 95.9 (69th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 95bp (steeper by 16bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (104bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 20 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 62/100 — Sticky, not accelerating in the core, but upside risk comes from breadth and energy. The underlying trimmed and median gauges sit near the middle of their history and mostly drift lower. Median CPI is 2.61 and trimmed-mean PCE 2.19, both falling. Sticky CPI (2.82) is flat. Flexible CPI is 6.12 and rising at its 82nd percentile, which is the oil shock feeding through. Dallas Fed breadth shows 28.9% of the PCE basket running above 5% (13.2% above 10% plus 15.7% at 5–10%), against 25.8% falling. That bimodal distribution is energy-driven rather than a broad wage-price spiral. Core PCE at 3.00759%, a 1y breakeven of 3.023% and 5y at 2.4174% say the market sees near-term pain but anchored medium-term expectations. Wages (AHE 3.0%, ECI 0.9) are not the problem. Persistence is moderate-to-elevated: too high for the Fed to cut, but not yet calling for hikes unless oil stays above $110.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (42x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The computed dot-com overlay has the current cycle at 243.0 at month 48 from the Oct-2022 anchor. That is below the 1994-anchored dot-com path at the same month (268.4) and far below its month-69 peak (665.3). Today's run looks like a solid bull market, not a melt-up. On the analyst-estimate side, the S&P 500 is highly concentrated (top-10 weight about 40%), and CAPE (about 39x) and market cap/GDP (about 215%) are near or above 2000 extremes on aggregate valuation. That contrasts with a computed Nasdaq trailing P/E of only 42.06x versus 175x in 2000. IPO froth is moderate (about 30/100): the mega-listings (SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic) talked about all year have not priced in the US, so supply is not flooding the market as it did in 1999–2000. Long-term EPS-growth expectations are elevated (about 70/100) on AI optimism, which is a BofA signpost worth watching. The precondition missing from 2000 is a central bank easing into froth: with a 10Y at 5.119% and core PCE at 3.0%, policy is a headwind rather than fuel. The five analyst-estimate inputs are judgment calls; they were not verified by web search this run.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

October 27–28 FOMC: hold expected (inference). Warsh refuses forward guidance, so expect no pre-signal. Core PCE at 3.0% rules out a cut, and inflation driven by energy plus soft payrolls (29k) argue against a hike unless oil climbs further.

~1 YEAR

Inference: a 'higher for longer, no promises' stance. We expect no cuts while core PCE stays near 3%, with a hike possible if the 1y breakeven (3.023%) climbs further. Communication stays minimal, so expect more market volatility around meetings. His long-standing preference for a smaller Fed balance sheet comes from his prior record and was not re-verified in this run's sources.

Reporting from late August says Warsh has sharply changed Fed communication by saying much less about the economy and inflation. He has said he does not want to give forward guidance on hikes, cuts or holds because it limits the Fed's flexibility. At his late-July press conference he caused confusion about his willingness to raise rates against stubborn inflation, and longer-term yields rose. His Jackson Hole speech was expected to focus on AI and productivity, demographics, and shocks from the Iran war. We could not verify post-Jackson Hole coverage. The 10Y at 5.119%, 13.18% above its 200DMA (computed), fits a market charging a term premium for that uncertainty (analyst inference).
